title: Consensus AI Pricing: Plans and Costs (2026 Guide)
summary: Consensus AI pricing includes a free tier for casual research and paid plans based on weekly work volume. Compare options to find the right fit.
body_markdown:
## Track Research Topics Alongside Consensus with Activepieces


Your Consensus limits should go only to questions that need them, and[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/) can take the rest. It is an open-source automation builder with a visual editor.


It can check PubMed and arXiv on a schedule, summarise what's new with an AI step, and post it to Slack or a spreadsheet.


That's the bootstrap version of topic tracking: it costs you an afternoon of setup instead of a seat.


The flow below runs left to right. A schedule trigger fires, PubMed and arXiv feeds supply new papers, an AI step summarises them, and the results land in a Slack channel and a spreadsheet row.


The point is that the researcher only reads a short digest, and the heavy search tool is never touched for routine watching.


Both PubMed and arXiv publish feeds for a saved search, which is what the trigger step reads. Run it daily or weekly, whichever matches how fast your field moves.


The Activepieces pricing page lists 1 credit per flow run, whatever the number of steps, so splitting that digest into a trigger, two feeds, a summary and two posts costs the same as a cramped two-step version.


Zapier's pricing page bills per task and Make's bills per module, so on those the same split costs more with every step you add.


A daily run is about 30 credits a month against the Free plan's 1,000, with unlimited flows; the AI summary step is the one exception, priced by the model you choose.


The spreadsheet keeps a searchable log, and Slack gives you the nudge. Activepieces can also be self-hosted, and its core is under the MIT licence, so the automation layer itself carries no licence fee if you're comfortable running it.


That covers monitoring. It doesn't replace judging evidence across papers, which is where Consensus earns its place.


Consensus (consensus.app) is the AI search engine for research papers: you ask a question and it surfaces what the literature says. Elicit (elicit.com) is the AI research assistant: it pulls structured details out of papers into tables.


Check each pricing page for current prices and caps before paying, since the figures here may change.


The decision rule is unchanged: pay for whichever one's deeper features you exhaust every week. If a digest from your workflow already answers your weekly need, neither upgrade is justified.


If all you need is summarised abstracts, a general model is plenty. Claude Haiku 5.5 is built for high-volume, latency-sensitive work, which suits a daily batch of abstracts, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 is the step up if summaries come out too thin.


The premium version is keeping one paid research seat for the weekly deep dive. Stay with the general assistant while your question is "what is new?" and move up only when it becomes "what does the evidence say?"
